title: 7  Explainer of Basis Expansion Models
text:
7.1 The Linear Model:
Suppose we measure two quantities, such as a child’s age (\(x\)) and child’s length (\(y\)) on many children. In regression (prediction modeling), we have a function \(f\) which takes in an input \(x\) and returns an average output at that input. The goal of prediction modeling is to learn \(f\) from data, so that for a new child we can predict their length using \(f(x)\).
Children of the same age do not all have the same length. We therefore write the observed length as the average length at that age \(f(x)\) plus the individual’s random deviation from that average, called the noise, \(\varepsilon\):
\[
\underbrace{y}_{\text{observed length of a child at age x}} = \underbrace{f(x)}_{\text{true average length of child at age x (unknown)}} + \underbrace{\varepsilon}_{\text{noise}}
\] We never observe \(f\) directly, so we estimate it from data and write the estimate as \(\hat f\). The predicted length of a child at age \(x\) is given by:
\[
\underbrace{\hat y}_{\text{predicted length at age } x}
=
\underbrace{\hat f(x)}_{\text{estimate of the average length at age } x}
\]
The gap between what we observed and what we predicted is the residual. It is our estimate of the noise \(\varepsilon\):
\[
\underbrace{\hat\varepsilon}_{\text{residual}}
=
\underbrace{y}_{\text{observed}}
-
\underbrace{\hat y}_{\text{predicted}}
\]
The true average \(f(x)\) is called the conditional mean. It is the expected (average) value of the outcome \(Y\), given the predictor value \(x\):
\[
E[Y \mid x] = f(x)
\]
The simplest choice of \(f\) is a straight line:
\[
f(x) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x
\]
With With \(p\) number of predictors \(x_1,\dots,x_p\) collected in a vector \(\mathbf{x}\), the straight line becomes a weighted sum:
\[
E[Y \mid \mathbf{x}]
= \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_1 + \cdots + \beta_p x_p
= \sum_{j=0}^{p} x_j\beta_j
= \mathbf{x}\boldsymbol\beta
\]
The numbers \(\beta_j\) are the model’s parameters (coefficients), and fitting the model means choosing them using the data.
The model also says how spread out the noise is around the average which is the conditional variance. We assume the spread is the same everywhere:
\[
\text{Var}(Y \mid \mathbf{x}) = \sigma^2 .
\]
For a single child \(i\), the model can be written out in full. This is called the scalar form:
\[
y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{ip} + \varepsilon_i,
\qquad \varepsilon_i \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} \text{Normal}(0,\ \sigma^2).
\] With \(n\) children we stack everything into vectors which can be represented as matrices:
\[
Y = X\boldsymbol\beta + \boldsymbol\varepsilon, \qquad
\boldsymbol\varepsilon \sim \text{Normal}(\mathbf{0}_n,\ \sigma^2 I_n).
\]
\[
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} y_1 \\ y_2 \\ \vdots \\ y_n \end{bmatrix}}_{Y\ (n\times 1)}
=
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}
1 & x_{11} & x_{12} & \cdots & x_{1p} \\
1 & x_{21} & x_{22} & \cdots & x_{2p} \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots \\
1 & x_{n1} & x_{n2} & \cdots & x_{np}
\end{bmatrix}}_{X\ (n\times (p+1))}
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} \beta_0 \\ \beta_1 \\ \vdots \\ \beta_p \end{bmatrix}}_{\boldsymbol\beta\ ((p+1)\times 1)}
+
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} \varepsilon_1 \\ \varepsilon_2 \\ \vdots \\ \varepsilon_n \end{bmatrix}}_{\boldsymbol\varepsilon\ (n\times 1)}
\]
\[
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} \varepsilon_1 \\ \varepsilon_2 \\ \vdots \\ \varepsilon_n \end{bmatrix}}_{\boldsymbol\varepsilon}
\sim
\text{Normal}\left(
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ \vdots \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{0}_n},\
\sigma^2
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & \cdots & 0 \\
0 & 1 & \cdots & 0 \\
\vdots & & \ddots & \vdots \\
0 & 0 & \cdots & 1
\end{bmatrix}}_{I_n\ (n\times n)}
\right)
\]

import numpy as np

# generates the predictor x. It draws 150 random variables (values) for age uniformly distributed between 0 and 36 months, so every age from birth to 3 years is equally likely.

# This is the true average function f(x) = E[Y|x]

    # true relations between child length and age is logarithmic

 # observed = true average + noise

section: 7.3 The Problem with a Straight Line:
text:
7.3 The Problem with a Straight Line:
The problem: a straight line is too rigid. The model \(f(x) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\) says that every extra month of a child’s age adds the same \(\beta_1\) cm of length, at every age. Real growth however, plateaus where the child may grow more rapidaly during the early months of infancy but for later months of infancy, they grow as a slwoer rate, creating a bending in the curve. A straight line cannot bend, so it will over-predict in some regions and under-predict in others, no matter how much data we collect. (A multiple linear regression is not a good fit).


Code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# straight-line (least squares) fit and its residuals
slope, intercept = np.polyfit(age, length_cm, 1)
resid = length_cm - (intercept + slope * age)
age_grid = np.linspace(0, 36, 200)

# average residual within age bins (a simple smooth)
edges = np.linspace(0, 36, 9)
centers = (edges[:-1] + edges[1:]) / 2
bin_means = [resid[(age >= lo) & (age < hi)].mean()
             for lo, hi in zip(edges[:-1], edges[1:])]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.8))

ax[0].scatter(age, length_cm, s=14, color="steelblue", alpha=0.6)
ax[0].plot(age_grid, intercept + slope * age_grid, color="darkorange", lw=3,
           label="Straight line")
ax[0].plot(age_grid, f_true(age_grid), "r--", lw=2, label="True average $f(x)$")
ax[0].set(xlabel="Age (months)", ylabel="Length (cm)", title="Straight-line fit")
ax[0].legend(loc="lower right", frameon=False)

ax[1].scatter(age, resid, s=14, color="steelblue", alpha=0.6)
ax[1].axhline(0, color="black", ls="--")
ax[1].plot(centers, bin_means, color="purple", lw=3, marker="o",
           label="Average residual per age bin")
ax[1].set(xlabel="Age (months)", ylabel=r"Residual $\hat{\varepsilon}$",
          title="Residuals of the straight line")
ax[1].legend(loc="lower center", frameon=False)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 7.1: Left: a straight line fit to curved growth data. Right: the residuals of that fit.





The straight line sits above the data at the youngest and oldest ages, so it over-predicts there (negative residuals). In the middle it sits below the data, so it under-predicts (positive residuals). If the line were a good model, the residuals would scatter randomly around zero. Instead the purple curve shows a systematic upside-down U pattern. This is the signal that the true relationship bends, and collecting more data will not fix it.

title: 7  Explainer of Basis Expansion Models
text:
7.4 Basis Expansion:
The key idea: The linear spline is a linear model, meaning it is linear in the parameters \(\boldsymbol\beta\) even though the relationship between the child’s length and age is not a straight line, so it is not linear in \(x\). The fitting method from the previous section only needs the model to be a weighted sum with the \(\beta\)’s as weights. It does not care what the quantities being weighted are. So instead of feeding the model \(x\) itself, we can feed it features of \(x\), called basis functions \(b_1(x), \dots, b_M(x)\). This is called a basis expansion:
\[
E[Y \mid x] = \beta_0 + \sum_{m=0}^{M} \beta_m\, b_m(x)
\]
\[
E[Y \mid x] = \sum_{m=0}^{M} \beta_m\, b_m(x), \qquad b_0(x) = 1.
\]
A basis function allows us to expand the predictor \(x\) into a vector of features \(\Phi(x) = \big(b_0(x), b_1(x), \dots, b_M(x)\big)'\) and build the curve as a weighted sum of them. Each basis function evaluated at the data becomes one column of the design matrix, with entries \(X_{im} = b_m(x_i)\). Everything else is unchanged:
\[
Y = X\boldsymbol\beta + \boldsymbol\varepsilon \quad\longrightarrow\quad Y = \Phi(X)\boldsymbol\beta + \boldsymbol\varepsilon, \qquad
\]
This works like building the point \((3,2)\) from the blocks \((1,0)\) and \((0,1)\) as \(3(1,0) + 2(0,1)\). The coefficients \(\beta_m\) say how much of each block to use. For example, the basis \(1, x, x^2\) builds every curve of the form \(\beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 x^2\). Each basis function evaluated at the data becomes one column of the design matrix \(X\).
Replacing \(x\) with basis functions \(b_0(x), \dots, b_M(x)\) changes only the columns of the design matrix. We write the expanded design matrix as \(\Phi\):
\[
\underbrace{X =  \begin{bmatrix}
1 & x_1 \\
1 & x_2 \\
\vdots & \vdots \\
1 & x_n
\end{bmatrix}}_{\text{raw design matrix } (n\times 2)}
\quad\longrightarrow\quad
\underbrace{\Phi(X) = \begin{bmatrix}
b_0(x_1) & b_1(x_1) & \cdots & b_M(x_1) \\
b_0(x_2) & b_1(x_2) & \cdots & b_M(x_2) \\
\vdots & \vdots & & \vdots \\
b_0(x_n) & b_1(x_n) & \cdots & b_M(x_n)
\end{bmatrix}}_{\Phi\ (n\times (M+1))}
\]
The entry in row \(i\) and column \(m\) is \(\Phi_{im} = b_m(x_i)\): basis function \(m\) evaluated at observation \(i\). The model keeps the same form:
\[
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} y_1 \\ y_2 \\ \vdots \\ y_n \end{bmatrix}}_{Y\ (n\times 1)}
=
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}
b_0(x_1) & b_1(x_1) & \cdots & b_M(x_1) \\
b_0(x_2) & b_1(x_2) & \cdots & b_M(x_2) \\
\vdots & \vdots & & \vdots \\
b_0(x_n) & b_1(x_n) & \cdots & b_M(x_n)
\end{bmatrix}}_{\Phi\ (n\times (M+1))}
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} \beta_0 \\ \beta_1 \\ \vdots \\ \beta_M \end{bmatrix}}_{\boldsymbol\beta\ ((M+1)\times 1)}
+
\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} \varepsilon_1 \\ \varepsilon_2 \\ \vdots \\ \varepsilon_n \end{bmatrix}}_{\boldsymbol\varepsilon\ (n\times 1)}
\]
that is, \(Y = \Phi\boldsymbol\beta + \boldsymbol\varepsilon\). Row \(i\) multiplies out to
\[
y_i = \beta_0 b_0(x_i) + \beta_1 b_1(x_i) + \cdots + \beta_M b_M(x_i) + \varepsilon_i,
\]
which is the weighted sum of basis functions plus noise. The least squares estimate has the same form as before, with \(\Phi\) in place of \(X\):
\[
\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (\Phi'\Phi)^{-1}\Phi'Y .
\]
Dimension check: \(\Phi'\) is \((M+1)\times n\), so \(\Phi'\Phi\) is \((M+1)\times(M+1)\), \(\Phi'Y\) is \((M+1)\times 1\), and therefore \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\) is \((M+1)\times 1\), one coefficient per basis function.
Example. The three children with ages \(2, 8, 18\) months respectively and the parabola basis \(b_0(x) = 1,\ b_1(x) = x,\ b_2(x) = x^2\):
\[
\begin{bmatrix} y_1 \\ y_2 \\ y_3 \end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 2 & 4 \\
1 & 8 & 64 \\
1 & 18 & 324
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix} \beta_0 \\ \beta_1 \\ \beta_2 \end{bmatrix}
+
\begin{bmatrix} \varepsilon_1 \\ \varepsilon_2 \\ \varepsilon_3 \end{bmatrix}
\]
Each piece only has to describe the data nearby, so the curve is flexible where it needs to be, local, and stable, and because it is still a basis expansion, it is still a linear in \(\boldsymbol\beta\) even though the curve is a parabola in \(x\).

title: 7  Explainer of Basis Expansion Models
text:
7.5 Types of Basis Functions:

7.5.1 Polynomials:
Take \(b_d(x) = x^d\), so that
\[
x \longrightarrow \{1,\ x,\ x^2,\ x^3,\ \dots,\ x^p\}, \qquad d = 0, 1, 2, \dots, p.
\] The model is a weighted sum of these powers:
\[
E[Y \mid x] = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 x^2 + \cdots + \beta_p x^p = \sum_{d=0}^{p} \beta_d\, x^d.
\]
This is not linear in \(x\) (it bends), but it is linear in \(\boldsymbol\beta\), so we can still use least squares, \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (\Phi'\Phi)^{-1}\Phi'Y\). The design matrix has one column per power of age:
\[
\Phi = \begin{bmatrix}
1 & x_1 & x_1^2 & \cdots & x_1^p \\
1 & x_2 & x_2^2 & \cdots & x_2^p \\
\vdots & \vdots & \vdots & & \vdots \\
1 & x_n & x_n^2 & \cdots & x_n^p
\end{bmatrix}
\]
The degree \(p\) controls flexibility. A degree 1 polynomial is a straight line, degree 2 is a parabola, and so on. Higher degree means a more flexible curve, but also more coefficients to estimate.


Code
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# create 200 evenly spaced ages from 0 to 36, in sorted order. The real age values are random and unsorted (would have looked like zigzag lines)
# the grid gives a smooth x-axis for drawing the fitted curves
age_grid = np.linspace(0, 36, 200)         

# function that takes ages x and a polynomial degree and returns the design matrix Phi
def poly_basis(x, degree):
    # create design matrix with columns 1, x, x^2, ..., x^degree
    # range(degree + 1) gives 0, 1, ..., p
    # The + 1 is there because range stops before its endpoint, and we want to include p
    # x**d for d in ... builds a list of vectors, x^0, x^1, x^2, ...., x^p. Each one is a column of Phi. Since$x^0 = 1, the first column is all ones, which is the intercept
    # np.column_stack puts those vectors side by side as columns, giving an n x (p+1) matrix
    return np.column_stack([x**d for d in range(degree + 1)])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 7))
ax.scatter(age, length_cm, s=14, color="purple", alpha=0.5, label="Data") # plot the 150 datapoints
ax.plot(age_grid, f_true(age_grid), "r--", lw=2, label="True $f(x)$") # Draws the true curve

# Repeats the next four lines once for each polynomial degree, so each pass fits and draws one curve
for degree in [1, 2, 3]:
    Phi = poly_basis(age, degree)  # builds the design matrix at your 150 observed ages. The shape is 150 x (p+1)
    beta_hat = np.linalg.lstsq(Phi, length_cm, rcond=None)[0] # least squares
    fit = poly_basis(age_grid, degree) @ beta_hat # predictions on grid
    ax.plot(age_grid, fit, lw=2, label=f"Degree {degree}") 

ax.set(xlabel="Age (months)", ylabel="Length (cm)", title="Natural polynomial fits")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.show()








Figure 7.2: Natural polynomials of degree 1, 2, 3, and 6 fit to the child growth data.





Key parts of the code

poly_basis(x, degree) builds the design matrix \(\Phi\). The list comprehension [x**d for d in range(degree + 1)] computes \(x^0, x^1, \dots, x^p\), and np.column_stack places each power in its own column. Since \(x^0 = 1\), the first column is the intercept.
Phi = poly_basis(age, degree) is \(\Phi\) evaluated at the 150 observed ages, so it has shape \(150 \times (p+1)\).
np.linalg.lstsq(Phi, length_cm, rcond=None)[0] solves the least squares problem and returns \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\). It computes the same answer as \((\Phi'\Phi)^{-1}\Phi'Y\) but in a numerically safer way than inverting a matrix directly.
poly_basis(age_grid, degree) @ beta_hat builds the basis on a smooth grid of ages and multiplies by \(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\). This is the weighted sum \(\sum_d \hat\beta_d x^d\), and the grid lets us draw a clean curve.

What we see. The straight line (degree 1) misses the bend, as before. Degree 2 captures some of it, and by degree 3 the fit is close to the true curve. Going to degree 6 improves the fit only slightly. The data are noisy and the true curve is smooth, so extra flexibility has little left to capture.

Pros:

no discontinuities
smooth curve

Cons:

It is a global function: every coefficient affects the whole curve (function), so changing one coefficient \(\beta_m\) changes \(f(x)\) everywhere, and data at one end of the range can change the fit at the other end. High-degree polynomials also tend to oscillate between data points and to diverge in the tails.




7.5.2 Linear Splines:
A linear spline fits a straight line on each segment of the \(x\)-axis and joins the lines at the knots \(K = k_1 <  k_2 <  \dots < k_K\), so the curve has no jumps.
The hinge function is a way to switch a the direction straight line on at a chosen point (creating a bend). Before the point it does nothing (it equals 0), and after the point it starts rising. It switches the direction of a straight line on at a chosen point \(k_K\) (the knot)
The point is the knot \(k\). The notation \((x - k)_+\) means “take \(x - k\), but if it is negative, use 0 instead.” The small \(+\) is shorthand for “keep only the positive part.” That is the same thing as \(\max(0,\ x - k)\), which picks the larger of 0 and \(x - k\).
\[
(x - k)_+ = \max(0,\ x - k) =
\begin{cases}
0 & x \le k \\
x - k & x > k.
\end{cases}
\]
It equals 0 until \(x\) reaches the knot, and after that it rises with slope 1. Because it starts at 0, it adds a bend to the curve without creating a jump. Adding one hinge per knot to the usual \(1\) and \(x\) gives the basis

\]
As before, this is linear in \(\boldsymbol\beta\), so we fit it with least squares. The design matrix has \(K + 2\) columns, one for each basis function.
For our example, knots = [6, 12, 24] has three knots, so \(K = 3\). The \(K + 2\) comes from counting the columns of the design matrix:

The “+ 2” is the intercept and the plain \(x\) column, which every linear spline has regardless of knots. The “\(K\)” part grows with the number of knots we add.
How to read the coefficients. The slope on each segment is a running total:

before the first knot, the slope is \(\beta_1\)
after \(k_1\), the slope is \(\beta_1 + \beta_2\)
after \(k_2\), the slope is \(\beta_1 + \beta_2 + \beta_3\), and so on.

So each hinge coefficient \(\beta_{j+1}\) is the change in slope at knot \(k_j\). This matches the earlier statement that knots control where the slope is allowed to change.

Pro:

no discontinuities
Is a local function since changes in coefficient \(\beta\) will change the specifc segment of the curve defined by the knots which are specific points which breaks up the x-axis into segments.

Cons:

not a smooth curve, has kinks (sharp corners).
Each hinge equals 0 at its own knot, so the pieces always meet. The slope, however, changes suddenly at each knot, which gives the curve a visible sharp corners. Cubic splines remove these corners.




Code
knots = [6, 12, 24] # we specify the location and amount of knots. A list of the ages (in months) where the slope is allowed to change

# create function that takes ages x and a list of knots and returns the design matrix Phi.
def linear_spline_basis(x, knots):
    # builds one hinge column per knot, (x - k)_+ = max(0, x - k)
    # np.maximum replaces every negative value with 0, so the hinge is 0 until the age passes the knot and then grows with slope 1
    hinges = [np.maximum(0, x - k) for k in knots] 
    return np.column_stack([np.ones_like(x), x] + hinges) # return the design matrix with columns 1, x, (x - k1)+, (x - k2)+, ...

Phi = linear_spline_basis(age, knots) # fits the desgin matrix n x (K + 2) = 150 observations x (K=3 knots + 2) = 150 x 5
beta_hat = np.linalg.lstsq(Phi, length_cm, rcond=None)[0] #solves the least squares problem to find beta hat and phi beta hat
fit = linear_spline_basis(age_grid, knots) @ beta_hat # rebuilds the same basis on the smooth, sorted grid of ages and multiplies by beta hat using matrix multiplication

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 7))
ax.scatter(age, length_cm, s=14, color="purple", alpha=0.5, label="Data")
ax.plot(age_grid, f_true(age_grid), "r--", lw=2, label="True $f(x)$")
ax.plot(age_grid, fit, lw=2.5, color="darkgreen", label="Linear spline")
for k in knots:
    ax.axvline(k, color="gray", ls=":", lw=1)
ax.set(xlabel="Age (months)", ylabel="Length (cm)", title="Linear spline fit")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.show()

Key parts of the code

knots = [6, 12, 24] are the points where the slope may change. Babies grow fastest early on, so we put more knots at young ages.
np.maximum(0, x - k) computes the hinge \((x - k)_+\) for every age at once. It returns 0 where \(x < k\) and \(x - k\) otherwise.
linear_spline_basis stacks the intercept column np.ones_like(x), the column x, and one hinge column per knot, giving \(K + 2\) columns. Only the basis function changed; the fitting lines (lstsq and then multiplying the grid basis by beta_hat) are the same as before.
np.cumsum(beta_hat[1:]) turns the coefficients into segment slopes. The first value is \(\beta_1\), the second is \(\beta_1 + \beta_2\), and so on, which is exactly the running total described in the math.
ax.axvline(k, ...) draws a dotted vertical line at each knot so the corners are easy to find.

What we see. The curve is made of four straight segments that join at the knots. The slope drops from about 3.5 cm per month before 6 months to about 1.4, 0.6, and 0.4 in the later segments, so the spline captures the “fast early growth, then leveling off” pattern that a single line misses. The typical gap between the spline and the true curve is about 1.0 cm, compared with 3.9 cm for the straight line.


7.5.3 Cubic Splines:
A cubic spline fits a cubic polynomial on each segment and joins the pieces so smoothly that the eye cannot see the knots. Using the same knots \(k_1 < \dots < k_K\) as before, the basis is
\[
x \longrightarrow \{1,\ x,\ x^2,\ x^3,\ (x - k_1)_+^3,\ (x - k_2)_+^3,\ \dots,\ (x - k_K)_+^3\},
\]
where \((x - k)_+^3 = \big(\max(0,\ x - k)\big)^3\). The model is
\[
E[Y \mid x] = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 x^2 + \beta_3 x^3 + \sum_{j=1}^{K} \beta_{3+j}\,(x - k_j)_+^3 .
\]
This has \(K + 4\) columns and is still linear in \(\boldsymbol\beta\), so we fit it with least squares.
Why cubed hinges? The linear spline used \((x - k)_+\), which has a corner at \(k\). Cubing it, \((x - k)_+^3\), makes the function start at the knot that it is flat there in three ways: its value, its slope, and its curvature (second derivative) are all 0 at \(x = k\). Adding it to the cubic polynomial before the knot therefore changes only the third-derivative term, so across each knot the curve has

the same value (no jumps),
the same slope (no corners),
the same curvature (no sudden change in bending).

This is why a cubic spline is called twice continuously differentiable and looks smooth.
Coefficients. Unlike the linear spline, the individual \(\hat\beta_j\) are hard to read directly. What matters is the fitted curve, not the coefficients.


Code
def cubic_spline_basis(x, knots):
    # design matrix with columns 1, x, x^2, x^3, (x - k1)+^3, (x - k2)+^3, ...
    hinges = [np.maximum(0, x - k) ** 3 for k in knots]
    return np.column_stack([np.ones_like(x), x, x**2, x**3] + hinges)

Phi_cub = cubic_spline_basis(age, knots) # n x (K + 4)
beta_cub = np.linalg.lstsq(Phi_cub, length_cm, rcond=None)[0]
fit_cub = cubic_spline_basis(age_grid, knots) @ beta_cub

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 7))
ax.scatter(age, length_cm, s=14, color="purple", alpha=0.5, label="Data")
ax.plot(age_grid, f_true(age_grid), "r--", lw=2, label="True $f(x)$")
ax.plot(age_grid, fit_cub, lw=2.5, color="steelblue", label="Cubic spline")
for k in knots:
    ax.axvline(k, color="gray", ls=":", lw=1)
ax.set(xlabel="Age (months)", ylabel="Length (cm)", title="Cubic spline fit")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.show()








Figure 7.4: Cubic spline with knots at 6, 12, and 24 months, compared with the linear spline.





Key parts of the code

np.maximum(0, x - k) ** 3 is the cubed hinge \((x - k)_+^3\). The ** 3 is the only difference from the linear spline code, apart from adding the columns x**2 and x**3.
cubic_spline_basis stacks \(1, x, x^2, x^3\) and one cubed hinge per knot, giving \(K + 4\) columns. With three knots that is 7 columns, compared with 5 for the linear spline.
The fitting steps (lstsq, then the grid basis times beta_cub) are unchanged. We again swapped the basis and kept the method.
The linear spline from the previous section is drawn in a faded green so the two can be compared.

What we see. The cubic spline follows the same overall shape as the linear spline, but the corners at the knots are gone and the curve bends smoothly. It is also closer to the truth: the typical gap between the fit and the true curve is about 0.55 cm, compared with 0.98 cm for the linear spline (and 3.9 cm for the straight line), using the same three knots. The cubic spline is slightly less accurate at the far right end of the range, where it overshoots the true curve by about 1.1 cm at 36 months, because there are no data beyond the last point to hold the tail in place. Natural splines, next, address this by forcing the tails to be straight.


7.5.4 Restricted Cubic Splines / Natural Cubic Splines:
A cubic spline can behave badly beyond the outermost knots, because past the last knot nothing holds the cubic in place and it can swing up or down. A restricted cubic spline (RCS) adds one rule to fix this:

The curve must be a straight line before the first knot \(k_1\) and after the last knot \(k_K\).

A cubic stops being a line when its \(x^2\) and \(x^3\) terms are non-zero, so this rule forces those two terms to vanish in each tail. That is 4 constraints in total (2 per tail), which removes 4 of the \(K + 4\) parameters of the ordinary cubic spline. An RCS with \(K\) knots therefore has only \(K\) columns (including the intercept), compared with \(K + 4\).
The basis is
\[
x \longrightarrow \{1,\ x,\ h_1(x),\ h_2(x),\ \dots,\ h_{K-2}(x)\},
\]
where, for \(j = 1, \dots, K - 2\),
\[
h_j(x) = (x - k_j)_+^3
- (x - k_{K-1})_+^3 \,\frac{k_K - k_j}{k_K - k_{K-1}}
+ (x - k_K)_+^3 \,\frac{k_{K-1} - k_j}{k_K - k_{K-1}}.
\]
The extra two terms subtract off exactly the cubic and quadratic growth that would otherwise appear after the last knot, so each \(h_j\) becomes linear there. In practice it is common to divide each \(h_j\) by \((k_K - k_1)^2\), which only rescales the columns and keeps the numbers a reasonable size.
The model is
\[
E[Y \mid x] = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \sum_{j=1}^{K-2} \beta_{j+1}\, h_j(x),
\]
and it is fit with least squares like every other basis.
The trade-off. The RCS uses fewer parameters and gives stable, straight tails, but it gives up flexibility at the edges. If the true curve is still bending at the ends of the data, a straight tail cannot follow it.


Code
def rcs_basis(x, knots):
    # design matrix: 1, x, h_1(x), ..., h_{K-2}(x)  (restricted cubic spline)
    t = np.asarray(knots, dtype=float)
    K = len(t)
    cube = lambda u: np.maximum(0, u) ** 3
    cols = [np.ones_like(x), x]
    for j in range(K - 2):
        h = (cube(x - t[j])
             - cube(x - t[K - 2]) * (t[K - 1] - t[j]) / (t[K - 1] - t[K - 2])
             + cube(x - t[K - 1]) * (t[K - 2] - t[j]) / (t[K - 1] - t[K - 2]))
        cols.append(h / (t[K - 1] - t[0]) ** 2) # rescale for numerical size
    return np.column_stack(cols)

knots_rcs = [1, 4, 10, 20, 32]

Phi_rcs = rcs_basis(age, knots_rcs)                                # n x K
beta_rcs = np.linalg.lstsq(Phi_rcs, length_cm, rcond=None)[0]
fit_rcs = rcs_basis(age_grid, knots_rcs) @ beta_rcs

# ordinary cubic spline with the same knots, for comparison
Phi_c5 = cubic_spline_basis(age, knots_rcs)                        # n x (K + 4)
beta_c5 = np.linalg.lstsq(Phi_c5, length_cm, rcond=None)[0]
fit_c5 = cubic_spline_basis(age_grid, knots_rcs) @ beta_c5

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 7))
ax.scatter(age, length_cm, s=14, color="purple", alpha=0.5, label="Data")
ax.plot(age_grid, f_true(age_grid), "r--", lw=2, label="True $f(x)$")
ax.plot(age_grid, fit_rcs, lw=2.5, color="darkorange", label=f"Restricted cubic spline ({Phi_rcs.shape[1]} columns)")
for k in knots_rcs:
    ax.axvline(k, color="gray", ls=":", lw=1)
ax.set(xlabel="Age (months)", ylabel="Length (cm)", title="Restricted cubic spline fit")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
plt.show()








Figure 7.5: Restricted cubic spline versus an ordinary cubic spline, both with knots at 1, 4, 10, 20, and 32 months.





Key parts of the code

cube = lambda u: np.maximum(0, u) ** 3 is a small helper for the cubed hinge \((u)_+^3\), so the formula for \(h_j\) stays readable.
The for j in range(K - 2) loop builds one column \(h_j(x)\) per knot except the last two. The three terms inside are the three pieces of the formula: the usual cubed hinge, minus the correction at the second-to-last knot, plus the correction at the last knot. The fractions are the weights from the math.
cols = [np.ones_like(x), x] starts with the intercept and the linear term, and np.column_stack puts all columns together. The result has \(K\) columns, which is why the legend shows 5 for the RCS and 9 for the cubic spline.
Dividing by (t[K - 1] - t[0]) ** 2 only rescales each column. It does not change the fitted curve.
The fitting steps are the same as in every earlier section. The ordinary cubic spline is refit with the same five knots so the comparison is fair.

What we see. The RCS follows the true curve nearly as closely as the cubic spline while using 5 columns instead of 9. The typical gap from the true curve is about 0.75 cm for the RCS and 0.69 cm for the cubic spline. The difference is in the tails. At 36 months the ordinary cubic spline overshoots the true curve by about 2.6 cm, while the RCS is off by only 0.6 cm, because its straight tail cannot swing away. At birth, both curves are still too high (by about 3.5 cm for the RCS and 4.1 cm for the cubic spline). The true curve bends sharply near 0 months, and neither fit has enough data or flexibility there to follow it.

8.2 Problem 1:
Confirm that OLS cannot create a unique solution for this dataset. Attempt to fit a linear model using lm() and report what happens. How many coefficients does R return as NA, and why?

# converts the matrix X into a dataframe d1
d1 <- as.data.frame(X)
# add y as an extra column in the dataframe named y
d1$y <- y 

# fit a linear model on the data (predict response y and using all columns in the datafraem d1 except the response y)
lm1 <- lm(y ~ ., data = d1) 

# extract all the coefficients in the data
beta_hat <- coef(lm1) 
# add a boolean mask where for coefficients which are not null (FALSE) and for coefficients which are null (TRUE)
beta_na <- is.na(beta_hat) 

# replace every null coefficient with 0
beta_hat[beta_na] <- 0 

# plot each coefficient where coefficients are black dots and null coefficients are red triangles
plot(beta_hat, col = beta_na + 1, pch = 16 + beta_na, xlab = "Coefficient index", ylab = expression(hat(beta))) 
# add a legend
legend("topright", legend = c("Estimated", "NA"), pch = 16:17, col = 1:2, bty = "n")
# add plot titles
title(main = paste("Coefficients set to NA:", sum(beta_na), "out of", length(beta_hat) - 1), font.main = 1)









length(coef(lm1)) # total coefficients the model in R tried to estimate

[1] 4089

sum(is.na(coef(lm1))) # how many came back NA

[1] 4018

sum(!is.na(coef(lm1))) # how many were actually estimated

[1] 71

lm1$rank # rank of the design matrix the model in R used

[1] 71

max(abs(residuals(lm1))) # how big is the largest error?

[1] 0

summary(lm1)$r.squared # how well does it "fit"?

[1] 1


Interpretation:
Of all 4,088 coefficients for the predictors and 1 coefficient for the intercept (resulting in 4,089 total coefficients), 4,018 were null while only 71 had values. Because the design matrix is n x p where p > n, this means that there are more features/measurements than there are number of samples. So, there are infinitely many solutions. These solutions are the individual coefficients we are interested in. So, since there were 71 samples, the linear model returned 71 valid coefficients however, for the remaining 4,018, these coefficients were returned as null. This is called a lack of identifiability. The design matrix table is therefore considered singular (not invertible).
The plot highlights this as we see all 71 data points along the 0 coefficient index, this is because all linearly dependent columns were arbitrarily dropped depending on their order present in the data and set to 0 (These columns are said to be redundant since they are linearly dependent on another column).

Recall that for the lasso penalty, the weaker weights are set equal to zero and thus, their corresponding features are dropped from the model. The ridge part introduces a grouping effect so correlated genes tend to share the weight and get similar coefficients. So, weights are kept or dropped together instead of one being picked arbitrarily. Therefore,

title: 9  Bayes Lasso Regression
text:
9.2 Laplace (double-exponential) Prior:
Tibshirani, who invented the lasso, noticed that the lasso answer is exactly the peak of the posterior if you use a particular prior: a Laplace (double-exponential) prior on each coefficient.
This prior is shaped like a tent, with a sharp spike at zero and tails that go out gently. It says “I believe most coefficients are probably near zero, but a few could be large.” That is the same idea as the lasso penalty, and the absolute-value penalty \(|\beta|\) is just the shape of that prior.
The Bayesian lasso of Park and Casella (2008) places the following prior on the regression coefficients:
\[
\pi(\boldsymbol{\beta} \mid \sigma^2)=\prod_{j=1}^{p}\frac{\lambda}{2\sqrt{\sigma^2}}\;e^{-\lambda|\beta_j|/\sqrt{\sigma^2}}
\tag{9.1}\]

9.2.1 Reading the equation
Left side, \(\pi(\boldsymbol{\beta} \mid \sigma^2)\). This is the prior. It says how plausible each possible value of \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) is before looking at any data, given the noise level \(\sigma^2\). Taller means more plausible.
The product \(\prod\). The coefficients for \(p\) predictors are treated as independent, so the prior for the whole vector is each coefficient’s prior multiplied together. That means we only need to understand one factor.
One factor. Writing \(\sigma = \sqrt{\sigma^2}\), a single coefficient has prior
\[
\frac{\lambda}{2\sigma}\;e^{-\lambda|\beta_j|/\sigma}.
\]

\(e^{-\lambda|\beta_j|/\sigma}\) is the tent shape.

At \(\beta_j = 0\) the exponent is 0, so \(e^0 = 1\) and the curve is at its highest.
As \(|\beta_j|\) grows, the exponent becomes more negative and the curve drops.
The absolute value makes the curve symmetric and gives it a sharp point at 0.

\(\frac{\lambda}{2\sigma}\) is a scaling constant. It makes the total area under the curve equal 1, which any probability density requires. It is also the height of the peak.
\(\lambda\) controls the sharpness. A bigger \(\lambda\) gives a taller, narrower tent, meaning you are more confident the coefficient is near 0.
\(\sigma\) controls the spread. Bigger noise \(\sigma\) widens the tent. Conditioning the prior on \(\sigma^2\) is the paper’s key design choice, and it guarantees that the posterior has a single peak.

Figure 9.1 shows this tent for three values of \(\lambda\), alongside the bell-curve prior that corresponds to ridge regression.


9.2.2 Properties of the Laplace (double-exponential) distribution

continuous probability distribution
sharp peak at its center
heavier tails than the normal (Gaussian) distribution



9.2.3 How the prior becomes the lasso penalty
By Bayes’ rule, the posterior is proportional to the likelihood times the prior:
\[
\pi(\boldsymbol{\beta} \mid \tilde{\mathbf{y}}, \sigma^2) \;\propto\;
\underbrace{\exp\!\left\{-\frac{\|\tilde{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_2^2}{2\sigma^2}\right\}}_{\text{likelihood}}
\;\times\;
\underbrace{\exp\!\left\{-\frac{\lambda}{\sigma}\sum_{j=1}^p |\beta_j|\right\}}_{\text{prior}}.
\]
Taking the negative log and multiplying by \(2\sigma^2\) gives
\[
\|\tilde{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_2^2 \;+\; 2\sigma\lambda \sum_{j=1}^p |\beta_j|.
\]

The likelihood contributes the sum of squared residuals.
The prior contributes a sum of absolute values, which is the \(L_1\) penalty.

The posterior peak (the mode) is the \(\boldsymbol{\beta}\) that minimizes this expression, which is exactly the lasso problem with penalty parameter \(2\sigma\lambda\). So the lasso estimate is the posterior mode under the Laplace prior. The Bayesian lasso goes further by using the entire posterior distribution, which provides credible intervals for each coefficient.


Show code
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from math import erf, sqrt

sigma = 1.0                      # noise standard deviation (set to 1 for the picture)
lams = [0.5, 1.5, 3.0]           # small, medium, large lambda
beta = np.linspace(-4, 4, 1000)  # possible coefficient values

blue, orange = "#2a78d6", "#eb6834"

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.8), sharey=True)

for ax, lam in zip(axes, lams):
    # Laplace prior, equation (3) for a single coefficient
    laplace = lam / (2 * sigma) * np.exp(-lam * np.abs(beta) / sigma)

    # Normal prior with the same variance as the Laplace (variance = 2*sigma^2/lam^2)
    sd = np.sqrt(2) * sigma / lam
    normal = np.exp(-beta**2 / (2 * sd**2)) / (sd * np.sqrt(2 * np.pi))

    # Shade the region |beta| < 0.5
    near0 = np.abs(beta) < 0.5
    ax.fill_between(beta[near0], laplace[near0], color=blue, alpha=0.18)

    ax.plot(beta, laplace, color=blue, lw=2.5, label="Laplace prior (lasso)")
    ax.plot(beta, normal, color=orange, lw=2, ls="--", label="Normal prior (ridge)")

    # Peak marker and label
    peak = lam / (2 * sigma)
    ax.plot(0, peak, "o", color=blue, ms=7, mec="white", mew=1.5)
    ax.annotate(f"sharp peak\nheight = λ/(2σ) = {peak:.2f}",
                xy=(0, peak), xytext=(25, 0), textcoords="offset points",
                fontsize=9, va="center", arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color="gray"))

    # Tail label
    ax.annotate("gentle tails", xy=(2.5, lam / (2 * sigma) * np.exp(-lam * 2.5 / sigma)),
                xytext=(0, 40), textcoords="offset points", ha="center", fontsize=9,
                arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color="gray"))

    # Probability that |beta| < 0.5 under each prior
    p_lap = 1 - np.exp(-lam * 0.5 / sigma)
    p_norm = erf(0.5 / (sd * sqrt(2)))
    ax.set_title(f"λ = {lam}\nP(|β| < 0.5): Laplace {p_lap:.0%}, Normal {p_norm:.0%}",
                 fontsize=10)
    ax.set_xlabel("Coefficient value (β)")
    ax.axvline(0, color="gray", lw=0.8, ls=":")
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

axes[0].set_ylabel("Prior plausibility (density)")
axes[0].legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=8, frameon=False)
axes[0].set_ylim(0, 1.9)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()








Figure 9.1: The Laplace (double-exponential) prior behind the lasso, compared with the normal prior behind ridge regression, for three values of λ. The Laplace density has a sharp peak at 0 and gentle tails.







9.2.4 How to read the picture

The x-axis is a possible value for one coefficient β.
The y-axis is how plausible the prior says that value is, so higher means more believable before seeing data.
The blue tent is the Laplace prior from equation (9.1). It peaks at β = 0 and falls off symmetrically on both sides.
The sharp point at 0 is the |β| in the exponent. This corner is what lets the posterior peak land exactly on zero, which gives the lasso its exact zeros.
The gentle tails mean a coefficient can still be large if the data push hard enough. The tent doesn’t forbid big values, it just considers them less likely.
The orange dashed curve is the normal (bell curve) prior that corresponds to ridge regression, drawn with the same overall spread. It is smooth and rounded at 0, so it has no corner to produce exact zeros. It also puts less weight on the far tails.
The shaded region and the two boxes show the “most coefficients are near zero” idea in numbers. The tent puts more of its probability within ±0.5 of zero than the bell curve does.



9.2.5 The Big Picture
Increasing \(\lambda\) makes the tent taller and narrower, so you’re more strongly betting that coefficients are near zero. In lasso terms, that is a bigger penalty and more coefficients dropped. Decreasing \(\lambda\) flattens the tent, which is a weaker penalty, and the lasso moves toward ordinary regression.

9.3 Choosing λ:
The lasso usually picks \(\lambda\) by cross-validation. The Bayesian version offers two alternatives:

Empirical Bayes (marginal maximum likelihood): choose the \(\lambda\) that makes the observed data most probable. It’s computed by repeatedly running the sampler and updating \(\lambda\).
Hyperprior: treat \(\lambda\) as another unknown, give it its own prior, and let the sampler estimate it along with everything else.

text:
9.5 The Bayesian lasso in Python with PyMC:
So far we have seen what the Bayesian lasso is. In this section we run it on real data.
The data. The riboflavin dataset has \(n = 71\) samples of the bacterium Bacillus subtilis. For each sample we have

the response \(y\): the log of the riboflavin (vitamin B2) production rate, and
\(p = 4{,}088\) predictors: the log expression level of each gene.

The question. Which genes are related to riboflavin production, and how sure are we about each one?
The challenge. We have far more predictors than samples (\(p \gg n\)). Ordinary regression cannot be fit here, so we need a method that shrinks coefficients, which is exactly what the lasso does. However, it shrinks groups of coefficients exactly to zero arbitrarily. How sure are we that these coefficients should be set exactly to zero? In other words, how sure are we that these predictors should be dropped from the model? We use the Bayesian Lasso which adds the ability to say how uncertain each coefficient is of having a certain value.

9.5.1 Step 1: Set up the tools
PyMC is a Python library for Bayesian modeling. You describe the model (priors and likelihood), and PyMC draws samples from the posterior for you. ArviZ is its companion library for diagnostics.

# imports
import numpy as np # import numpy
import pandas as pd # import pandas
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt # import matplotlib
import pymc as pm # import pymc
import arviz as az # import arviz
from sklearn.linear_model import LassoCV # import lasso from scikit-learn

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)  # fixed seed of 42 so results are reproducible

9.5.2 Step 2: Move the data from R to Python
The data came as an .rds file, which is R’s own file format. The file holds a data frame with the response y and a \(71 \times 4088\) matrix x of gene expression values. We convert it to a plain CSV file that Python can read. This only needs to be run once, in R.
rib <- readRDS("riboflavin.rds")

# x is stored as a special "AsIs" matrix; unclass() turns it into a plain matrix
X <- unclass(rib$x)

# Put y in the first column, then all 4,088 gene columns
write.csv(cbind(y = rib$y, X), "riboflavin.csv", row.names = FALSE)


9.5.3 Step 3: Look at the data

df = pd.read_csv("riboflavin.csv")

y_all = df["y"].to_numpy() # response: log riboflavin production
X_df = df.drop(columns="y") # predictors: one column per gene
gene_names = X_df.columns.to_numpy()
X_all = X_df.to_numpy()

n, p = X_all.shape

print(f"Genes (p):   {p}")

Samples (n): 71
Genes (p):   4088


Notice that \(p = 4088\) is about 58 times larger than \(n = 71\). With more predictors than observations, there are infinitely many coefficient vectors that fit the data perfectly, so ordinary least squares has no unique answer. The prior is what makes the problem solvable: it says “most coefficients are probably near zero.”


9.5.4 Step 4: Prepare the data
We do three things before modeling.
4a. Split into training and test sets. We fit the model on the training samples and keep some samples hidden. Later we use the hidden samples to check whether the model predicts well on data it has never seen.
4b. Standardize. We rescale every gene to mean 0 and standard deviation 1, and center and scale \(y\). This matters because the lasso penalty treats all coefficients equally, so predictors measured on larger scales would otherwise be penalized unfairly. Centering also lets us leave the intercept out of the model, since centered data have an intercept of zero (the paper makes the same simplification). Test data are scaled using the training means and standard deviations.


Code
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

# 4a. 80/20 split (20% of 71 samples rounds up to 15 test samples)
# X_train_raw: gene values for the training samples (56 × 4088)
# X_test_raw: gene values for the test samples (15 × 4088)
# y_train_raw: the response for the training samples (56 values)
# y_test_raw: the response for the test samples (15 values)

X_train_raw, X_test_raw, y_train_raw, y_test_raw = train_test_split(
    X_all, y_all, test_size=0.2, random_state=42
)

# 4b. Standardize genes - means and sds come from TRAINING data only
# We keep all 4088 genes (no screening step); the Bayesian lasso handles p > n.

x_scaler = StandardScaler().fit(X_train_raw)
Z_train = x_scaler.transform(X_train_raw)
Z_test = x_scaler.transform(X_test_raw)

# Standardize y the same way (we keep y_mean and y_sd to convert predictions back later)

y_mean, y_sd = y_train_raw.mean(), y_train_raw.std(ddof=1)
y_train = (y_train_raw - y_mean) / y_sd
y_test = (y_test_raw - y_mean) / y_sd

n_train, p = Z_train.shape
n_test = len(y_test)
print(f"Training samples: {n_train}, test samples: {n_test}, genes: {p}")


Training samples: 56, test samples: 15, genes: 4088




9.5.5 Step 5: Build the model
A Bayesian model has two parts: a likelihood (how the data arise given the parameters) and priors (what we believe about the parameters beforehand). The model mirrors the paper:








Piece
Math
PyMC code




Likelihood
\(y_i \sim N\left(\mathbf{x}_i^\top \boldsymbol{\beta},\ \sigma^2\right)\)
pm.Normal("y_obs", mu=..., sigma=sigma, observed=y_train)


Prior on each coefficient
\(\beta_j \mid \sigma^2 \sim \text{Laplace}\left(0,\ \sigma/\lambda\right)\), which is equation (3)
pm.Laplace("beta", mu=0, b=sigma / lam)


Prior on the noise
\(\sigma \sim \text{Half-Cauchy}(1)\)
pm.HalfCauchy("sigma", beta=1)


Prior on the penalty
\(\lambda^2 \sim \text{Gamma}(r, \delta)\), as in Section 3.2 of the paper
pm.Gamma("lam_sq", alpha=r, beta=delta)



A few notes on these choices:

The Laplace scale. The Laplace density \(\frac{1}{2b}e^{-|\beta|/b}\) matches equation (3) when \(b = \sigma/\lambda\). Because \(b\) depends on \(\sigma\), the prior is conditional on the noise level, which is the paper’s key design choice for getting a single-peaked posterior.
Letting the data choose \(\lambda\). Instead of fixing \(\lambda\) or tuning it by cross-validation, we give it a prior (a “hyperprior”) and let the sampler estimate it along with everything else. The paper puts the Gamma prior on \(\lambda^2\). We use \(r = 1\), which makes it an exponential prior, and a small \(\delta = 0.01\), which makes it very diffuse (prior mean for \(\lambda^2\) is \(r/\delta = 100\)). A diffuse prior means the data, not our guess, drive the result.


# Hyperprior settings for lambda^2 ~ Gamma(r, delta)  (rate parameterization)
r, delta = 1.0, 0.01

with pm.Model(coords={"gene": gene_names}) as bayes_lasso:

    # Penalty strength. We place the prior on lambda^2 as in the paper.
    lam_sq = pm.Gamma("lam_sq", alpha=r, beta=delta)
    lam = pm.Deterministic("lam", pm.math.sqrt(lam_sq))

    # Noise standard deviation (the data are standardized, so ~1 is the right scale)
    sigma = pm.HalfCauchy("sigma", beta=1.0)

    # One coefficient per gene, each with a Laplace (tent-shaped) prior.
    # Scale b = sigma / lambda, matching equation (3).
    beta = pm.Laplace("beta", mu=0.0, b=sigma / lam, dims="gene")

    # Predicted mean for each training sample: X times beta
    mu = pm.math.dot(Z_train, beta)

    # Likelihood: observed y is the prediction plus normal noise
    pm.Normal("y_obs", mu=mu, sigma=sigma, observed=y_train)



9.5.6 Step 6: Sample from the posterior
The posterior distribution has no neat formula, so we simulate it. MCMC (Markov chain Monte Carlo) is a method that wanders through the space of possible parameter values, spending more time where the posterior is high. After enough steps, the list of visited values behaves like a random sample from the posterior.

A chain is one such wandering path. We run 4 chains from different starting points so we can check that they agree.
Tuning steps (tune) let the algorithm adapt its step size. They are thrown away. This is the “burn-in” in the paper.
Draws (draws) are the samples we keep.

This takes a few minutes on a laptop.

    idata = pm.sample(
        draws=1000,          # samples kept per chain
        tune=1000,           # warm-up steps per chain (discarded)
        chains=4,            # independent chains
        target_accept=0.95,  # smaller steps: slower but safer for this tricky geometry
        random_seed=42,
        progressbar=False,   # keeps the rendered book tidy

In Figure 9.2, healthy sampling looks like four overlapping curves on the left and a fuzzy band with no trends on the right. If you see large R-hat values, many divergences, or chains that disagree, increase tune, increase target_accept (up to 0.99), or run longer.


9.5.8 Step 8: Read the results
First, pull the samples out of the result object into plain arrays. Each row of beta_draws is one posterior draw of all the coefficients.

post = idata.posterior

# beta_draws has shape (number of draws, number of genes)
beta_draws = (post["beta"]
              .stack(sample=("chain", "draw"))
              .transpose("sample", "gene")
              .values)
lam_draws = post["lam"].values.flatten()
sigma_draws = post["sigma"].values.flatten()

print("beta_draws shape:", beta_draws.shape)

beta_draws shape: (4000, 4088)



9.5.8.1 8a. What did the data say about \(\lambda\)?

lam_lo, lam_med, lam_hi = np.quantile(lam_draws, [0.025, 0.5, 0.975])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 3.5))
ax.hist(lam_draws, bins=40, color="#2a78d6", alpha=0.8)
ax.axvline(lam_med, color="black", lw=1.5, label=f"median = {lam_med:.1f}")
ax.set_xlabel("λ")
ax.set_ylabel("Number of posterior draws")
ax.legend(frameon=False)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
plt.show()

print(f"λ: median {lam_med:.2f}, 95% credible interval ({lam_lo:.2f}, {lam_hi:.2f})")







Figure 9.3: Posterior distribution of the penalty parameter λ. The prior was very diffuse, so this shape comes from the data.





λ: median 10.00, 95% credible interval (2.88, 23.39)


A single number from ordinary lasso (chosen by cross-validation) is replaced here by a whole distribution for \(\lambda\). Remember that a larger \(\lambda\) means a sharper tent, so a stronger pull toward zero.


9.5.8.2 8b. Coefficients with credible intervals
For each gene we compute the posterior median (our best guess) and a 95% credible interval (the range that contains the coefficient with 95% probability, given the model and data). The paper’s rule for variable selection is: a gene looks important if its interval excludes zero.

coef_lo, coef_med, coef_hi = np.quantile(beta_draws, [0.025, 0.5, 0.975], axis=0)
excludes_zero = (coef_lo > 0) | (coef_hi < 0)

results = pd.DataFrame({
    "gene": gene_names,
    "median": coef_med,
    "lower_95": coef_lo,
    "upper_95": coef_hi,
    "excludes_zero": excludes_zero,
}).sort_values("median", key=np.abs, ascending=False)

print(f"Genes whose 95% interval excludes zero: {excludes_zero.sum()} of {p}\n")
print(results.head(10).round(3).to_string(index=False))

Figure 9.4: Posterior medians and 95% credible intervals for the 20 genes with the largest effects. Orange intervals exclude zero; gray ones include zero.





Two things are worth noticing:

No coefficient is exactly zero. The Bayesian lasso reports posterior medians, which are shrunken toward zero but not set to zero. The credible intervals take over the job of variable selection.
Many intervals include zero, even for genes with large estimates. With only 56 training samples and 100 candidate genes, the data cannot pin most coefficients down. This is an honest answer, and it is something the ordinary lasso would not tell you.



9.5.8.3 8c. What a posterior looks like
For the presentation, it helps to see the thing the Bayesian lasso returns for each gene: a whole distribution, not a single number.

strongest = results.iloc[0]["gene"]
weakest = results.iloc[-1]["gene"]

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.5), sharex=True)
for ax, g in zip(axes, [strongest, weakest]):
    j = np.where(gene_names == g)[0][0]
    ax.hist(beta_draws[:, j], bins=40, color="#2a78d6", alpha=0.8)
    ax.axvline(0, color="black", lw=1.2, ls="--")

    ax.set_xlabel("Coefficient (standardized units)")

Figure 9.5: Full posterior distributions for the strongest gene (left) and a gene with a weak effect (right). The dashed line marks zero.








9.5.9 Step 9: Compare with the ordinary lasso
We now fit the ordinary lasso on the same training data, choosing its penalty by 5-fold cross-validation, and compare coefficients.
scikit-learn writes the lasso objective as \(\frac{1}{2n}\|y - X\beta\|_2^2 + \alpha\|\beta\|_1\). Starting from the posterior and dividing through, the Bayesian \(\lambda\) corresponds to \(\alpha = \sigma\lambda / n\). This lets us translate our posterior into the lasso’s units.

lasso = LassoCV(cv=5, random_state=0, max_iter=50_000).fit(Z_train, y_train)

alpha_equiv = np.median(sigma_draws) * lam_med / n_train

Figure 9.6: Ordinary lasso coefficients versus Bayesian lasso posterior medians. The two are strongly related, but the lasso has many exact zeros (points on the vertical line at 0) while the Bayesian medians do not.





Correlation: 0.272


This matches what the paper found on its diabetes data: the Bayesian lasso posterior medians are very close to the lasso estimates, with the added benefit of credible intervals, and with no exact zeros.

title: 11  Class-conditional bivariate normal distribution
text:
The simulated dataset generates binary classes with equal probability of 50% each:

\(P(Y = 0) = P(Y = 1) = 0.5\) Where predictor vectors follow class-conditional bivariate normal distributions:
\(X \mid Y=0 \sim \mathcal{N}_2((-1,0)^T, \mathbf{I})\)
\(X \mid Y=1 \sim \mathcal{N}_2((1,0)^T, \mathbf{I})\)

Equal Priors: \(P(Y = 0) = P(Y = 1) = 0.5\)

What it means: There are two groups/classes in your dataset: Class 0 and Class 1.
Plain English: You have an equal 50/50 chance of picking a point from Class 0 or Class 1 (like flipping a fair coin).

Predictor Vectors: \(X = (X_1, X_2)\)

What it means: Every single observation (data point) has two measurable features/variables, which you can plot as an \((x, y)\) point on a standard 2D graph.
Plain English: Instead of predicting something based on a single number, the model looks at a coordinate pair on a 2D plane to decide if it belongs to Class 0 or Class 1.

Class-Conditional Normal Distributions: \(\mathcal{N}_2(\boldsymbol{\mu}, \mathbf{I})\)

What it means: The data points for each class form a rounded, bell-curve-shaped “cloud” or cluster around a central center point (mean vector \(\boldsymbol{\mu}\)).
Mean centers (\(\boldsymbol{\mu}\)):

Data points for Class 0 cluster around the point \((-1, 0)\) on the graph.
Data points for Class 1 cluster around the point \((1, 0)\) on the graph.

Identity Covariance Matrix (\(\mathbf{I}\)):

The two features \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) are independent of each other (non-correlated).
The variance (spread) is 1 in all directions.
Plain English: The data points spread out equally in every direction, creating two neat, circle-shaped clouds of dots centered at \((-1, 0)\) and $(1, 0


Visualizing the Setup - Imagine a 2D scatter plot:

You place a target at \((-1, 0)\) for Class 0 (e.g., blue dots) and throw darts around it.
You place another target at \((1, 0)\) for Class 1 (e.g., red dots) and throw darts around it.
Because the distance between \(-1\) and \(1\) is only \(2\) units, the two clouds of dots overlap in the middle near \(x = 0\).
Fisher’s Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) tries to draw a straight line right down the middle (around \(x = 0\)) to separate the blue dots from the red dots as accurately as possible.

title: 12  Cross Validation
text:
In a Cross Validation:

The specific machine learning model is trained using the training data.
The trained machine learning model is then tested/evaluated using testing data which is the data it did not train on.
IMPORTANT NOTE:

Seeing how the model works on data it was not been trained on allows us to evaluate how well the model performed. So, within each iteration, the same data used to train the model should not be used to test that version of the model.
Therefore, the data needs to be split into a training dataset and a testing dataset.


For example, in a 4-fold cross valdiaiton, we divide a dataset up into 4 equally sized folds. We may choose to use the first 75% of the data (first 3 folds of data) to train a particular machine learning model then use the last 25% of the data (last fold of the data) to test the machine learning model. However, how do we know if this selection of data is the best option? what if using the first 25% of the data for testing the model and the last 75% for training the model is better?

Cross validation helps identify and evaluate overfitting by using various combinations of data folds for training the model and keeps track of how well the model performed using the corresponding testing data folds. So, instead of splitting a dataset just once into a training set and a testing set, cross validation repeats the process multiple times.

IMPORTANT NOTE:

Model overfitting is a modeling error that occurs when a machine learning model matches its training data too closely, which leads it to simply memorizing the data, random noise, and minor quirks instead of actually learning from the data to idenfity meaningful, true, general patterns.
Cross validation can help address overfitting concerns by providing a reliable estimate of how well a model performs on unseen data rather than just memorizing the training set.

title: 13  Bootstrapping
text:
The statisics for each of the bootstrapped datasets are taken. This could include the mean, median, standard deviation, etc.
For simplicity, lets assume we are only considering the mean of each of the boootstrapped datasets. After collecting all the means for all bootstrapped datastes. These means can be plotted onto a histogram which is used to visualize the frequency of a particular measurment or statistic.
This histogram which is a distribtuion of bootstrap statisics, in our case, distribution of bootstrap means, gives us an idea of how much our statistic might vary if we could repeatedly obtain new samples from the same population.
This histrogram can also provide insight into the liklihood of getting something close to the original statisic, in our case the mean, of the original dataset when the experiment is rerun multiple times by looking at the distribution of the histrogram.
The standard deviation of the bootstrap distribution of the statistic from the histogram provides an estimate of the standard error of that statistic of the original dataset.
We can also determine a bootstrap confidence interval which can be constructed from the distribution of bootstrap estimates. For example, a 95% bootstrap confidence interval provides a range of plausible values for the population parameter based on the bootstrap distribution where The interval contains 95% of the bootstrap estimates.
This can allow us to conduct a hypothesis test to determine whether we reject or fail to reject the nu,ll hypothesis.
